head:
Health · Society

The price of a sedentary life: health and economy

Sedentary behaviour is often presented as a personal matter. It is also a cause of disease that researchers try to put numbers on, and a line of spending for health systems. These figures circulate widely, rarely with their method. This article rebuilds them one by one, from the whole population to the limits of the models, to answer one question: how much does it really cost, and what is avoidable?

The problem

“Sedentary behaviour costs billions.” You have probably read a sentence like this, with a figure attached. It almost always comes without the three pieces of information needed to assess it: what is counted, how the calculation was done and what it assumes.

First, two words need to be told apart. Physical inactivity means not meeting the activity recommendations: 150 to 300 minutes per week of moderate intensity, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous intensity, or an equivalent combination. Sedentary behaviour means the time spent awake sitting or lying down, with very low energy expenditure, measured in hours per day.12 You can train for an hour and then sit for eight: you are then active and sedentary at the same time. Most cost studies deal with inactivity, and each step specifies which one it is talking about.

Next, a cost figure can count care alone, add lost work to it, or put a euro value on lost years of life. A figure for “attributable” deaths is the result of a calculation that rests on assumptions, not a count. Two figures keep coming back since a WHO report of 2022: nearly 500 million new cases of disease by 2030, and 27 billion dollars a year.1 We will trace their source, what they count and what they do not.

The question

What is the price of sedentary behaviour in health and in money, how much of that price is avoidable, and what can you do at your own level?

We move in six steps, from the broadest to the finest: the people concerned, the attributed deaths, one person’s risk, the costs, the projections, and then what remains fragile in these calculations.

What is at stake

What is at stake for you comes down to five things.

Health first: the models we will read link inactivity to coronary heart disease, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, several cancers, dementia and depression.2

Lifespan next. The estimates are counted in years gained at the level of one person and in hundreds of thousands of deaths at the level of the world.

Money, which concerns you even if you stay in good health. In the first global estimate that separates the payers, the public sector funds 31.2 of the 53.8 billion international dollars of care attributed to inactivity.7 This care is largely pooled.

Finally, the direction of travel. In 2022, 31% of the world’s adults did not meet the recommendations, about 5 points more than in 2010, and the trend leads to 35% in 2030 if nothing changes.5 A worsening slope is not corrected by a single good year.

One last stake is a matter of judgement. An overstated figure promises savings that will not come, an understated figure suggests there is no urgency. Knowing what each figure measures lets you decide without being wrong in either direction.

Step 1 of 6 · The population concerned

A growing share of adults does not meet the recommendations

Everything else is calculated by multiplying a risk by a number of people. So we start with that number. According to the WHO, 31% of the world’s adults, about 1.8 billion people, did not reach the recommended activity levels in 2022. That is about 5 points more than in 2010. If the trend continues, the share would reach 35% in 2030, far from the target of reducing inactivity by 15% by 2030.1,5 The gaps between regions are wide, from 14% in Oceania to 48% in high-income Asia-Pacific, and women (34%) are more affected than men (29%).5

These figures use the WHO threshold, which counts endurance only. In France, the answer changes depending on the threshold used. In the Esteban survey (2014-2016, 2,682 adults aged 18 to 74), 71% of men and 53% of women meet the endurance recommendation, which leaves 29% and 47% below it.13 ANSES, with the INCA3 survey (1,305 adults aged 18 to 64), applies three benchmarks at once: endurance, strength training and flexibility, each in duration and in frequency.14

In France, the share of inactive people runs from fewer than one in three to almost everyone, depending on the threshold

Percentages of adults. * Complements to 100% of the published 71% and 53%, therefore calculated. Different populations and questionnaires: we are comparing definitions, not a change over time. Sources: Esteban (Santé publique France), INCA3 (ANSES).13,14

What this means

With the endurance benchmark alone, fewer than one man in three and a little fewer than one woman in two are below it. With the three ANSES benchmarks together, 95% of adults do not meet all of them. The population has not changed; the bar has moved. When you read “X million inactive people”, look for the threshold. The WHO cost estimates use endurance alone, which counts fewer people than the broad definition.3

On the sedentary behaviour side, adults spend on average 6 h 39 a day sitting or lying down (7 h 30 among 18-39 year olds, Esteban survey), and 38% exceed 8 hours a day according to ANSES.12,14

What remains is to see how many deaths are attributed to these people, and what “attributing” assumes.

Step 2 of 6 · Attributable mortality

Attributing deaths to inactivity rests on a calculation, not on a count

The reference estimate dates from 2012. Lee and colleagues calculated, country by country, the share of several diseases attributable to inactivity, with what they call conservative assumptions.6 Worldwide, they attribute to it 6% of the burden of coronary heart disease, 7% of type 2 diabetes, 10% of breast cancers and 10% of colon cancers. It would account for 9% of premature deaths, that is more than 5.3 million out of 57 million deaths worldwide in 2008. If inactivity were eliminated, world life expectancy would gain 0.68 years (from 0.41 to 0.95).6

Worldwide, inactivity is linked to 6 to 10% of the cases of several diseases

Attributable fractions, world, 2008 data. Bar: world estimate. Line: range published by the authors. Source: Lee et al., The Lancet, 2012 (abstract).6

The word “attributable” comes from a formula that combines two ingredients: the share of the population that is exposed (here, the inactive) and the extra risk that the exposure brings. With 31% of people inactive worldwide and a 20 to 30% higher risk of death among people who are insufficiently active, an order of magnitude given by Santé publique France,12 the formula gives between 5.8% and 8.5% of deaths. This is an illustrative calculation made for this article, not a published estimate. It falls in the same zone as the 9% of Lee and the 7.2% of a more recent study of 168 countries, reported by the specialist press.18 The WHO speaks of 4 to 5 million deaths a year.12 The estimates differ depending on the year, the definition of inactivity and the relative risks used.

What this means

“Attributable” means: deaths that would not have occurred, on average, if inactivity disappeared, assuming the link is causal and nothing else changes. It is not a number of people who died from having been inactive. At the scale of a population, it serves to size the problem. At your scale, it does not tell you your personal probability, which depends on your age, your history and your baseline risk.

The same paper quantifies what a partial reduction in inactivity would bring: a 10% reduction would avoid more than 533,000 deaths a year, a 25% reduction more than 1.3 million.6 These figures are proportional (10% of 5.3 million is about 530,000) and more realistic than “eliminating inactivity”, which would assume that everyone moves. According to this model, a modest fall in inactivity already amounts to hundreds of thousands of deaths a year.

For France, the most quoted official figure is more than 38,000 deaths and 62,000 diseases attributable per year, taken from a 2022 France Stratégie report that Santé publique France and the Ministry of Sports repeat.12,15 The original report could not be consulted, and the documents that repeat it do not describe its method.

For sedentary behaviour, an analysis of 54 countries cited by ONAPS associates more than 3 hours a day sitting with 3.8% of deaths, independently of activity level.17 This second-hand figure is not additive with the previous ones.

What does this mean for one person, and how much movement is needed for the risk to change?

Step 3 of 6 · What is avoidable for one person

The first levels of activity are the ones that lower the risk the most

To measure what can be avoided, you need a dose-response curve: risk as a function of the amount of activity. Two large cohorts provide one.

The first pools six American and European cohorts: 661,137 adults with a median age of 62, 116,686 deaths, 14.2 years of follow-up. Compared with those who do no leisure-time activity, those who stay below the recommended minimum have a 20% lower risk of death (risk ratio of 0.80). Between one and two times the minimum, it is 31% lower (0.69), then 37% lower between two and three times the minimum (0.63). Beyond three to five times the minimum, the gain is small, with no rise in risk up to ten times the minimum.11 This minimum is 7.5 MET-hours per week, or about 150 minutes of moderate activity (calculation: 2.5 hours at 3 METs; the MET expresses effort as multiples of resting energy expenditure).

The second covers 416,175 people followed in Taiwan for 8 years on average. Those who do about 15 minutes of activity a day (92 minutes per week) have a 14% lower risk of death than the inactive. Each additional 15-minute block lowers the risk by a further 4%, up to about 100 minutes a day, after which the authors see no more gain.10 In life expectancy at age 30 compared with the inactive, the low-volume group gains about 2.6 years (men) and 3.1 years (women), and those who meet the recommendation 4.2 and 3.7 years.10

Each level of activity reduces the risk of death, the first the most

Adjusted risk ratios multiplied by 100 (no activity = 100), therefore derived. Study 2: volumes of 3.75 to 7.49, 7.5 to 16.49, 16.5 to 25.49 and 25.5 MET-h per week or more. Sources: Arem et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 2015; Wen et al., The Lancet, 2011.10,11

What this means

In both studies, the first level is the most worthwhile. Going from nothing to a little removes 20 points of risk in the first study (from 100 to 80), and the next level removes 11. For a person starting from zero, the aim is not to reach 150 minutes to get an effect, it is to begin. What cannot be claimed is that activity alone produces the whole gap: activity is self-reported by the participants, and those who are able to move more are also, on average, in better health. Step 6 returns to this.

The Taiwanese sample is rather socio-economically favoured, which the authors flag as a limit to generalisation.10

The price in health is set. The price in money is calculated differently, and the words matter even more there.

Step 4 of 6 · What it costs

The price in money: direct costs, indirect costs, social cost

Three families of figures get mixed up in the press. Direct costs are care (consultations, hospital stays, medicines), paid by public insurance, private insurers and households. Indirect costs are lost output: missed working days, lives of working-age people cut short. The “social cost” is a broader term, found in official French figures, whose method needs checking.

The first global estimate that separates these items dates from 2016. Ding and colleagues estimated the cost of inactivity in 2013 for 142 countries, or 93.2% of the world population, and for five diseases: coronary heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, breast and colon cancers.7,8 The total is 67.5 billion international dollars (a unit that corrects for price differences between countries). It breaks down into 53.8 billion of care and 13.7 billion of lost output. Of the care, the public sector funds 31.2 billion, private insurers 12.9 and households 9.7. Type 2 diabetes alone accounts for 70% of direct costs.7

In the global figure for 2013, care weighs far more than lost output

Billions of international dollars, 2013, 142 countries, five diseases. 31.2 + 12.9 + 9.7 = 53.8; 53.8 + 13.7 = 67.5. Source: Ding et al., The Lancet, 2016 (University of Sydney press release).7

What this means

Care weighs about four times more than lost output (53.8 against 13.7, calculated ratio). More than half of care (31.2 out of 53.8, or 58%, calculated) is paid by the public sector, and therefore by contributions and taxes. Rich countries bear 80.8% of the care costs, whereas low- and middle-income countries carry the largest share of the disease.8

These direct costs represent on average 0.64% of health spending worldwide and 0.84% in North America.8 The authors consider their figures rather underestimated, for lack of data in many countries.7

In France, the official figure is a social cost of 140 billion euros a year, set against more than 38,000 deaths and 62,000 diseases. It comes from a France Stratégie report of March 2022 on the socio-economic evaluation of public health investment projects.12,15 The documents that repeat it specify neither the share of care, nor that of lost output, nor the method.16 It exceeds Ding’s global total, which covers five diseases: the two figures probably do not have the same scope, for example because a social cost can put a value on lost years of life. This point could not be verified, and it is better to read this figure as a social value than as spending by the national health insurance. Among the sources open for this article, no report from the Cour des comptes and no Inserm expert review puts a figure on this cost.

These costs are those of 2013. The figures circulating today are projections to 2030.

Step 5 of 6 · The projections

Projections to 2030: what the 500 million cases and the 27 billion really count

In 2022 the WHO took up the results of a study published in The Lancet Global Health (Santos et al., 2023), the first global estimate of new cases of disease linked to inactivity and of their cost to public health systems.1,2 The method is the same attributable fraction as above, applied to 194 countries and 13 health conditions: coronary heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dementia, depression and seven cancers.2,3

If the share of inactive people stays what it is, the study counts 499.2 million new cases between 2020 and 2030.3,4 These are cases of disease, and the same person can have several. Almost half are hypertension (234.6 million, 47%), 43% depression and anxiety (215.7 million), and 74% would occur in low- and middle-income countries.3 This is the “nearly 500 million” of the WHO report.1

The cost to public systems is 523.9 billion international dollars over 2020-2030, or 47.6 billion a year. In current US dollars, that makes 301.8 billion in total, or 27.4 billion a year.3 The WHO’s “27 billion dollars a year” and the 47.6 billion are therefore the same estimate expressed in two units.1,3

This cost covers only public health spending, only for new cases, and only first-year treatment. It excludes households, private insurers, long-term care, complications, mortality and productivity losses.3 It is therefore not “the cost of sedentary behaviour”: it is the cost of the first year of treatment of new cases borne by the public sector.

A small number of cases can account for a large share of the costs

2020-2030 projection, constant share of inactive people. * Complement to 100% of the 63% borne by high-income countries, therefore calculated. Sources: Santos et al., The Lancet Global Health, 2023 (abstract and summary sheet).2,3

What this means

Cases are not all equal. Dementia makes up 3% of new cases but 22% of costs, cancers 1% of cases and 15% of costs, type 2 diabetes 2% of cases and 9% of costs.2 Low- and middle-income countries account for 74% of cases, whereas high-income countries bear 63% of costs. Dividing 27 billion by 500 million would give a “cost per case” that does not exist.

The authors also give the size of their doubt: when the relative risk is varied between its bounds, the number of cases ranges from 154 to 860 million and the cost from 182 to 900 billion international dollars over the period.3

What, in these calculations, could be wrong, and in which direction?

Step 6 of 6 · Objections and uncertainties

What could distort the calculations, and in which direction

Objection 1: the methods do not give the same order of magnitude

Take the share of health spending linked to inactivity in North America. Ding’s study (five diseases, attributable fraction) gives 0.84%.8 A 2015 American study (Carlson and colleagues) compares the spending of insufficiently active adults with that of active adults, all health conditions combined, and finds 11.1% of total spending (interval from 7.3 to 14.9%).9

Two methods give two orders of magnitude for the share of health spending

Share of total health spending associated with inactivity. Line: 95% confidence interval given by Carlson et al. Different scopes: Ding, world and North America; Carlson, United States. Sources: Ding et al., The Lancet, 2016; Carlson et al., Progress in Cardiovascular Diseases, 2015.8,9

What this means

The gap, a factor of about thirteen (11.1 divided by 0.84, calculated ratio), comes from the method. Ding counts only five diseases and applies relative risks taken from the literature. Carlson counts all the associated spending, which also captures differences that do not come from inactivity. Neither is “the right one”: they answer two neighbouring questions. Keep the range rather than a single figure.

Objection 2: sick people move less, so it would be the illness that costs

This is reverse causation. When the adults who report difficulty walking are removed from Carlson’s calculation, the share goes from 11.1% to 8.7% (from 5.2 to 12.3).9 Part of the spending associated with inactivity is therefore that of people whom illness prevents from moving. The gap, 2.4 points or about a fifth of the initial figure (calculated), gives an order of magnitude of the bias, not its value: excluding walking difficulties does not remove silent diseases. The same problem arises in the cohorts of step 3, where a person who falls ill moves less before dying.

Objection 3: the model’s assumptions

The attributable fraction assumes that the relationship is causal, that the relative risk taken from the literature applies everywhere, and that eliminating inactivity would not change the other risk factors, which the authors of the 2023 study themselves consider unlikely.3 The cost per case in low- and middle-income countries is extrapolated from European and English data.3 The variants tested (step 5) give the size of the doubt, not its direction.

Objection 4: avoiding cases is not saving money, and not everything pushes upward

The 523.9 billion is not a possible saving. The authors specify that these are not net avoidable costs: they model neither the cost of programmes to get people moving, nor an efficacy below 100%.3 If you hear “moving would avoid 500 billion”, none of these studies supports it. The errors do not all go in the same direction either: the 2023 study counts only the first year of treatment and public spending, and only endurance, so real inactivity is probably higher.3 Ding and colleagues also describe their estimate as conservative.7 The causal assumptions may push the figures upward, the exclusions downward, and the studies read do not allow us to say which dominates.

The answer to the problem

The question had three parts: the price in health and in money, the avoidable share, and what you can do. Here are the answers, with their certainty.

What is solid. Inactivity goes together with more deaths and more disease in every source read, and the link follows a dose: the risk falls from the very first levels (0.80 below the recommended minimum, 0.86 for about 15 minutes a day). At the scale of the world, the models attribute to inactivity 7 to 9% of deaths, that is 4 to 5.3 million a year depending on the estimate. The share of insufficiently active adults is rising.

What is probable. The order of magnitude of care costs: tens of billions of international dollars a year worldwide (53.8 billion in 2013 for five diseases and all payers; 47.6 billion a year in projection for first-year public costs alone), plus production losses (13.7 billion in 2013). We cannot say whether these estimates are too low or too high.

What is not established. A single figure. The 500 million cases and the 27 billion describe a specific scenario. For France, the 140 billion euros is a social cost whose method and share of care are unknown. The truly avoidable share of the costs is also unknown: the 523.9 billion is not savings.

At the level of one person, the answer is clearer than on money. The data show an associated benefit from the first minutes of activity, subject to reverse causation. The price is paid first in individual risk. A collective price exists too, in tens of billions of dollars a year in the studies read, without it being possible to fix it precisely.

What to put in place

Nothing that follows depends on the billions: it rests on what the studies show at the level of one person. The retest frequency is an editorial choice, not a study result.

  1. Measure your starting point.Take the test on this page: it places your fitness on the day. It does not tell you how much you move during the week: for that, note your minutes of activity and your hours sitting for seven days.
  2. Aim for a first level.If you are below the recommendations, start with about fifteen minutes a day: this level is associated with a 14% lower risk of death in Taiwan, and a level below the recommended minimum with a 20% lower risk in the American cohort.10,11 These are associations, not a promise.
  3. Work up towards the benchmarks.The official benchmarks are 150 to 300 minutes per week of moderate intensity, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous intensity, with strength training at least two days a week; the French version asks for 30 minutes a day.12 Beyond three to five times the minimum, the American cohort shows almost no further gain.11 Aiming higher can serve performance; the data read do not require it for longevity.
  4. Know your sitting time.The French average is 6 h 39 a day, and ANSES counts separately those who exceed 8 hours.12,14 The sources read do not say what reduction changes the risk: start by knowing your own figure.
  5. Retest every 8 to 12 weeks, under the same conditions.Same surface, same time of day, same warm-up. Between two tests, keep a log of your minutes and your hours sitting.

A known illness, chest pain or unusual breathlessness justify medical advice before you increase the intensity.

What these figures do not say
  • The links with mortality come from observational studies, with activity self-reported by the participants. An undetected illness can explain both low activity and a death.
  • The cost models cover neither the same diseases, nor the same payers, nor the same years: their results are not additive.
  • The official French figures are read in documents that cite them, not in the original report. Lee, Ding, Wen, Arem and Santos are known through their abstract, a press release or the specialist press, not through their full text.

Frequently asked questions

Are the 500 million cases and the 27 billion a year reliable?

They do come from the study by Santos and colleagues, and they do not contradict each other: 499.2 million cases, and 27.4 billion US dollars a year, or 47.6 billion international dollars.1,3 They describe a specific scenario: neither the total cost of sedentary behaviour, nor a possible saving.

Is the French figure of 140 billion euros established?

Santé publique France and the Ministry of Sports cite it, attributing it to France Stratégie (2022). The method and the share of care do not appear there. It is better read as a social cost than as a health expenditure.12,15

How long do you need to move for it to count?

In the two cohorts read, the risk of death is already lower for about 15 minutes a day than with no activity, and it keeps falling up to about three times the recommended minimum.10,11
